```{r, include=FALSE}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readxl)
library(httr)
library(rvest)
```

<!-- Feel free to modify the subsection names -->

# Data

The CIA World Factbook provides basic intelligence on the history,
people, government, economy, energy, geography, environment,
communications, transportation, military, terrorism, and transnational
issues for 266 world entities.

In this case study you will work with world data from 2020 which
contains information on

-   median age
-   youth unemployment rate
-   net migration rate (difference between the number of persons
    entering and leaving a country during the year per 1,000 persons -
    based on midyear population)

for most world entities. The data was downloaded from
<https://www.cia.gov/the-world-factbook/about/archives/>. For data
manipulation, `dplyr` functions should be used. For importing data, any
package can be used.

# Tasks

## a) Data loading

```{=html}
<!-- Load in R the following data sets which you can find in TUWEL. For each data set, ensure that missing
values are read in properly, that column names are unambiguous. Each data set should contain at the end
only two columns: country and the variable.
- rawdata_343.txt which contains the (estimated) median age per country. Pay attention! The delimiter
is 2 or more white spaces (one space would not work as it would separate country names which contain
a space); you have to skip the first two lines. Hint: you can look into function read.fwf or the readr
corresponding function. It might also be useful to use tidyr functions to unite some columns back or
separate them.
- rawdata_373.csv which contains the (estimated) youth unemployment rate (15-24) per country
- rawdata_347.txt which contains (estimated) net migration rate per country. -->
```
```{r, message=FALSE}
data343_location <- "../data/rawdata_343.txt"
data373_location <- "../data/rawdata_373.csv"
data347_location <- "../data/rawdata_347.txt"

# Load data
# Define the widths of the fields
pos343 <- fwf_positions(start = c(9, 75), end = c(74, 79))
pos347 <- fwf_positions(start = c(9, 72), end = c(71, 79))

# Read files into dataframes
rawdata_343 <- read_fwf(data343_location, col_positions = pos343)
rawdata_373 <- read_csv(data373_location)
rawdata_347 <- read_fwf(data347_location, col_positions = pos347)
# Drop first 2 rows
rawdata_343 <- rawdata_343[-c(1, 2), ]
rawdata_347 <- rawdata_347[-c(1, 2), ]

# Set the column names
colnames(rawdata_343) <- c("country_name", "median_age")
colnames(rawdata_347) <- c("country_name", "net_migration_rate")
```

## b) Merging datasets

```{=html}
<!-- Merge the data sets containing raw data using dplyr function on the unique keys. Keep the union of all
observations in the tables. What key are you using for merging? Return the dimension of the merged data
set. -->
```
```{r}
# Merge the data sets
rawdata <- merge(rawdata_343, rawdata_347, by = "country_name", all = TRUE)
rawdata <- merge(rawdata, rawdata_373, by = "country_name", all = TRUE)

# Return the dimension of the merged data set
print(dim(rawdata))
```

## c) External info extraction

```{=html}
<!-- You will acquire more country level information such as the classification of the country based on income.
Such an information can be found at https://datahelpdesk.worldbank.org/knowledgebase/articles/906519.
From there extract the classification for 2020 into low/lower-middle/upper-middle/high income countries. -->
```
```{r, message=FALSE}
# Read the xlsx file
income_classification <- read_excel("../data/OGHIST.xlsx", sheet = "Country Analytical History")
# Extract relevant information. That is:
# All elements from the 11th row and the column which at the 5th row has value 2020
# And the respective country name, which is on the 2nd column
country_classification <- income_classification[11:228, c(1, 2, which(income_classification[5, ] == 2020))]
colnames(country_classification) <- c("country_code", "country_name", "income_status")
```

## d) Merging yet again

```{=html}
<!-- Merge this information to the data set in b.
1. What are the common variables? Can you merge using them? Why or why not?
2. A reliable merging for countries are ISO codes as they are standardized across data sources. Download the
mapping of ISO codes to countries from https://www.cia.gov/the-world-factbook/references/country-data-codes/ 
and load it into R.
3. Merge the data sets using the ISO codes. -->
```
```{r, message=FALSE}
# Merge the data sets
rawdata_wrong <- merge(rawdata, country_classification, by = "country_name", all = TRUE)

# Load country codes
raw_ccodes <- read_csv("../data/Country Data Codes.csv")

# Join raw_ccodes by Name with rawdata by country_name
# From raw_ccode, get only GENC column
rawdata <- left_join(rawdata, raw_ccodes[, c("Name", "GENC")], by = c("country_name" = "Name"))

# Now join can be done by country_code
rawdata <- left_join(rawdata, country_classification[, c("country_code", "income_status")], by = c("GENC" = "country_code"))
```

## e) More external info introduction

```{=html}
<!-- Introduce into the data set information on continent for each country and subcontinent (region). You should
find a way to gather this data. You can find an appropriate online resource, download the data and merge
the information with the existing data set. Name the merged data set df_vars. -->
```
```{r, message=FALSE}
continent_table_web <- "https://statisticstimes.com/geography/countries-by-continents.php"

# Read the html
response <- httr::GET(continent_table_web) 
continent_table <- content(response, as="text") %>%
  rvest::read_html() %>%
  rvest::html_nodes("#table_id") %>%
  rvest::html_table(na.strings = "")
# Extract to a table
continent_table <- continent_table[[1]]

# Add information of continent, region and sub-region to the rawdata
# Join by ISO-alpha3 Code and GENC
df_vars <- left_join(rawdata, continent_table[, c("ISO-alpha3 Code", "Continent", "Region 1", "Region 2")], by = c("GENC" = "ISO-alpha3 Code"))
df_vars <- rename(df_vars, Region_1=`Region 1`, Region_2=`Region 2`)
```

## f) Discuss tidyness

```{=html}
<!-- Discuss on the tidyness of the data set df_vars. What are the observational 
units, what are the variables?
What can be considered fixed vs measured variables? Tidy the data if needed. -->
```
It can be said that the dataframe is already tidy. This is because each
row represents a country and each column represents a variable.
Variables are the country name, median age, net migration rate, youth
unemployment rate, income status classification, continent, region and
sub-region. The observational units, or samples, are the countries. All
*fixed* variables are categorical. They are: <u>country_name</u>,
<u>GENC</u>, <u>Continent</u>, <u>Region 1</u> and <u>Region 2</u>. The
measured variables are <u>median_age</u>, <u>net_migration_rate</u>,
<u>youth_unempl_rate</u> and <u>income_status</u>.

## g) Frequency table

<!-- Make a frequency table for the status variable in the merged data set. Briefly comment on the results. -->

```{r, message=FALSE}
df_vars %>% 
  group_by(income_status) %>%
  summarise(n = n())
```

Among the identified income statuses:

-   **High income (H)**: This is the most common income status, with 79
    countries falling into this category.
-   **Lower middle income (LM)**: This is the second most common income
    status, with 54 countries falling into this category.
-   **Upper middle income (UM)**: This is the third most common income
    status, with 52 countries falling into this category.
-   **Low income (L)**: This is the least common income status, with
    only 27 countries falling into this category.
-   Missing values: There are 15 countries for which we have no
    information about income status.

The distribution suggests a hierarchy, with a larger number of countries
classified as high income, followed by lower middle income, upper middle
income, and finally low income.

## h) Distribution of income status per continent

```{=html}
<!-- What is the distribution of income status in the different continents? Compute the absolute frequencies as
well as the relative frequency of status within each continent. Briefly comment on the results. -->
```
```{r, message=FALSE}
freqs <- df_vars %>%
  group_by(Continent, income_status) %>%
  summarize(absolute_frequency = n()) %>%
  group_by(Continent) %>%
  mutate(relative_frequency = absolute_frequency / sum(absolute_frequency) * 100)

print(freqs)
```

Observations:

-   **Africa**: The majority of countries fall into the lower-middle
    (42%) and low-income (42%) categories, with a relatively smaller
    proportion in the upper-middle (13%) and high-income (2%)
    categories.

-   **Asia**: There is a diverse distribution across income categories,
    with significant representation in the high-income, the lower-middle
    and upper-middle income categories. Only 8% of the countries in Asia
    are in the low-income category.

-   **Europe**: The majority of European countries are classified as
    high-income (71%), reflecting the economic development and stability
    of many European nations. However, there are also some countries in
    the lower-middle and upper-middle income categories. There are no
    countries in the low-income category.

-   **North America**: The distribution is relatively balanced across
    income categories, with notable representation in all categories,
    even though the most significant category is the high-income
    countries (47%).

-   **Oceania**: Similar to North America, there is a diverse
    distribution across income categories in Oceania. While high-income
    countries are well-represented, there are also countries in the
    lower-middle and upper-middle income categories.

-   **South America**: The majority of South American countries fall
    into the upper-middle income category (67%), with fewer countries
    classified as low-middle income (8%).

## i) Identify "lone" countries

```{=html}
<!-- From h. identify the countries which are the only ones in their respective group. Explain in few words the
output. -->
```
```{r, message=FALSE}
# Filter countries that are the only ones in their respective income status group within each continent
unique_countries <- freqs %>%
  filter(absolute_frequency == 1, !is.na(Continent), !is.na(income_status))

print(semi_join(df_vars, unique_countries))
```

These results indicate the countries that are the sole representatives
of their respective income status groups within each continent:

1.  **Bolivia**:
    -   **Continent**: South America
    -   **Income Status**: Lower middle income (LM)
    -   **Explanation**: This suggests that Bolivia is the poorest
        country in South America.
2.  **Seychelles**:
    -   **Continent**: Africa
    -   **Income Status**: High income (H)
    -   **Explanation**: Seychelles stands out as the only high-income
        country within the continent of Africa. This highlights its
        relatively high level of economic development compared to other
        African nations.
3.  **Ukraine**:
    -   **Continent**: Europe
    -   **Income Status**: Lower middle income (LM)
    -   **Explanation**: This suggests that Ukraine is the poorest
        country in Europe.

## j) Number of sub-regions

```{=html}
<!-- For each continent count the number of sub-regions in the data set. How granular are the subcontinents that
you employ in the analysis? -->
```
```{r, message=FALSE}
# Group by continent and count the number of unique sub-regions
subregion_counts <- df_vars %>%
  group_by(Continent) %>%
  summarize(
    num_subregions_1 = n_distinct(Region_1),
    num_subregions_2 = n_distinct(Region_2)
  )

print(subregion_counts)
```
We observe that Africa exhibits the highest level of granularity among the continents, characterized by the most sub-regions present at both a less granular level (Region 1) and a more detailed level (Region 2). Europe and North America display a moderate level of granularity, with 4 and 3 first-level sub-regions respectively, and 2 second-level sub-regions each. In contrast, South America shows the least granularity, with only 1 sub-region present at both the first and second levels.

## k) Distribution of income status per sub-region

```{=html}
<!-- Look at the frequency distribution of income status in the subregions of Nort- and South-Americas. Comment
on the results. -->
```
```{r, message=FALSE}
# Filter the dataframe for subregions of North and South Americas, 
# group by subregions and calculate the frequency distribution of income status
subregion_income <- df_vars %>%
  filter(Continent %in% c("North America", "South America"), !is.na(income_status)) %>%
  group_by(Continent, Region_1, Region_2, income_status) %>%
  summarize(count = n())

print(subregion_income)
```
We observe a notable disparity in income status between North American and South American countries within the shared region of Latin America and the Caribbean. In North America, high-income countries dominate, with 14 instances, followed by upper-middle-income countries totaling 11 (7+4), and lastly, lower-middle-income countries with 5 (1+4) cases. Conversely, in South America, the distribution is distinct, with upper-middle-income countries prevailing at 8, compared to only 2 high-income countries. This divergence underscores significant differences in economic profiles between the two continents, even within the same regional context.

## l) Deeper into income status in America

```{=html}
<!-- Dig deeper into the low-middle income countries of the Americas. Which ones are they? Are they primarily
small island states in the Caribbean? Comment. -->
```
```{r, message=FALSE}
# Filter the dataframe for subregions of North and South Americas, 
# group by subregions and calculate the frequency distribution of income status
lowincome_subregions <- df_vars %>%
  filter(Continent %in% c("North America", "South America"), income_status == "LM")

print(lowincome_subregions)
```
The low-middle income countries of the Americas include Belize, Bolivia, El Salvador, Haiti, Honduras, and Nicaragua. These countries are primarily located in Central America and the Caribbean. While some of these countries are indeed small island states in the Caribbean, such as Haiti, others like Belize, El Salvador, Honduras, and Nicaragua are part of Central America. This indicates that the classification of low-middle income is not exclusive to small island states but also applies to countries within the Central American region.
